title: Pork Carcass and Offal Inspection Process

lessons.title: Inspecting pigs on a working line
lessons.html:
The pork line

Pigs are stunned, bled, scalded, dehaired and then eviscerated. Because the skin stays on, the carcass surface needs careful inspection. In this work experience module you inspect pigs at line speed under a qualified inspector.

Head inspection

  • View the head, throat and tonsil area.
  • Incise the submandibular lymph nodes for abscesses and tuberculosis-type lesions.
  • Incise the cheek (masseter) muscles and examine the tongue for pork measles.

Offal inspection

  • Lungs: view and palpate for pneumonia, pleurisy and abscesses. Condemn lungs that took in scalding water.
  • Heart: view, open and incise for measles cysts and pericarditis.
  • Liver: view and palpate for milk spots, abscesses and hydatid cysts.
  • Spleen and kidneys: look for swelling and small dark red spots.
  • Intestines: view with the mesenteric lymph nodes.

Carcass inspection

  • View the skin for erysipelas diamonds, bite wounds, bruising and hair left after dehairing.
  • View the inside: pleura, peritoneum, diaphragm and spine.
  • Check joints and look at cut muscle for measles and pale, soft, watery meat.

Hygiene on a pork line

Scalding and dehairing can push dirt and water into the carcass. Watch for scald water in the lungs and dirt in skin folds, ears and feet. Hair and scurf must be removed before evisceration. Sterilise your knife between carcasses and after any abscess.

Safety

Pork lines are wet and fatty, so floors are slippery. Wear non-slip boots and your protective glove. Be aware of hot water and steam near the scalding tank.

lessons.title: Common pork findings and judgement
lessons.html:
Conditions you will meet

FindingUsual action
Pneumonia and pleurisyCondemn lungs; strip affected pleura
Milk spot liverCondemn liver
Tail-bite abscessTrim; check the spine for spread; detain if spread
Lymph node abscess in the headCondemn the head or affected part; check carcass
Erysipelas skin lesionsDetain if acute or with fever signs
Pork measles cystsDetain for veterinarian
ArthritisTrim affected joint and surrounding area; detain if many joints
Bruising and fight woundsTrim

Pork measles: a public health priority

Pork measles (Cysticercus cellulosae) is the cyst stage of the human tapeworm Taenia solium. People who swallow its eggs can develop cysts in their brain. Pigs raised in free-range village conditions, with access to human faeces, are at the highest risk. Inspect the cheek muscles, tongue, heart and diaphragm carefully on every pig. Detain all carcasses with cysts and follow the veterinarian's judgement under the regulations.

Notifiable disease alert

African swine fever has caused outbreaks in South Africa. If you see a batch with widespread haemorrhages in lymph nodes and kidneys, enlarged dark spleens, or many sick pigs in the lairage, stop and report to the veterinarian immediately. Keep the batch, its trucks and equipment apart until the veterinarian gives instructions.

Detention

Tag the carcass and all parts, move them to the detention rail and report. Do not remove evidence before the final decision.

lessons.title: Records and producer feedback for pigs
lessons.html:
Using pork inspection records

Pig production is intensive, and small changes in health have big financial effects. Your records help producers and the state.

Record for each lot

  • Producer, date and number of pigs.
  • Number of lungs condemned for pneumonia and pleurisy.
  • Number of livers condemned for milk spots.
  • Tail-bite and fight lesions.
  • Measles, erysipelas and any detentions with final judgements.
  • Notifiable disease reports.

What feedback can achieve

  • High pneumonia rates point to poor ventilation, overcrowding or a herd disease the farmer's vet should investigate.
  • Milk spots point to a need for better roundworm control and hygiene in pens.
  • Tail biting points to stress, overcrowding, boredom or feed problems.
  • Pork measles points to free-roaming pigs and poor sanitation, and needs action with local animal health and health services.

State veterinary services use this information for disease surveillance under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.

Your logbook

Record each day the number of pigs inspected, the stations worked and findings. Ask your mentor to sign off each station when you can do it independently at line speed. Note detentions and their outcome.

Key points

  • Inspect the skin carefully because it stays on the pig carcass.
  • Incise the submandibular lymph nodes and cheek muscles on every pig.
  • Detain all carcasses with pork measles cysts.
  • Report suspected African swine fever immediately and keep the batch apart.
  • Lot records on pneumonia, milk spots and tail biting help farmers improve their herds.
